Hot
hŏt
adj. (of great heat; of wrath, kindled; of Laodicea's water, fervent; rendering Hebrew charah, cham, and chamam, Greek zestos)
Old English hāt. The Hebrew verbs of anger in the Old Testament are verbs of heat; wrath does not rise, it waxes hot.

Biblical Definition

Wrath is hot: “let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them” (Exo 32:10), and Moses answers, “LORD, why doth thy wrath wax hot against thy people?” (Exo 32:11). Manna melted “when the sun waxed hot” (Exo 16:21). Solomon asks, “Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?” (Pro 6:28). David's silence broke because “my heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned” (Psa 39:3). Ephraim's adulterers “are all hot as an oven” (Hos 7:7). And to Laodicea: “thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth” (Rev 3:15–16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hot as having sensible heat, opposed to cold; ardent in temper; violent; furious; vehement; eager.

expand to see more

HOT, a. Having sensible heat; opposed to cold; as a hot stove or fire; a hot cloth; hot liquor.

2. Ardent in temper; easily excited or exasperated; vehement.

3. Violent; furious; as a hot engagement.

4. Eager; animated; brisk; keen; as a hot pursuit.

Key Scripture

Rev 3:15 — "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot."

Rev 3:16 — "So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth."

Exo 32:10 — "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation."

Psa 39:3 — "My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue,"

Pro 6:28 — "Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?"

Hos 7:7 — "They are all hot as an oven, and have devoured their judges; all their kings are fallen: there is none among them that calleth unto me."

Modern Corruption

Laodicea's hot and cold are read as zeal and hostility, which makes Christ prefer an enemy to a lukewarm friend.

expand to see more

The common reading of Revelation 3:15 has Christ wishing the Laodiceans were either on fire for Him or openly against Him, and then has to explain why He would prefer open hostility. He would not. The city's water is the picture: Hierapolis across the valley had hot springs, Colossae had cold ones, and Laodicea's supply arrived by aqueduct tepid and foul, fit only to be spat out. Hot water heals and cold water refreshes; both are useful, and lukewarm water is useful for nothing. The rebuke is uselessness. A church can be doctrinally respectable, financially comfortable (“I am rich, and increased with goods”), and good for nothing to anyone, and that is the church He threatens to spue out.

“My wrath may wax hot” is filed under the God of the Old Testament, as if Revelation 3:16 were a different temperature. It is the same heat in the mouth of the Lamb. Moses' intercession in Exodus 32 is worth watching for what it does not do: he never denies that the wrath is just. He pleads the covenant, the Name, and the fathers, and God repents of the evil. The intercessor who begins by explaining why the people did not deserve it has not read Moses.

Psalm 39:3 is the discipline of the heated heart. David resolved to keep silence “even from good,” his sorrow was stirred, his heart was hot within him, and the fire burned — “then spake I with my tongue.” He spoke to God. The verses that follow are prayer, not complaint to men, and the whole psalm is a model for what to do with a heart that has reached temperature: take it to the one hearer who can bear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew charah (H2734), to burn, be kindled (of anger); cham (H2525) and chamam (H2552), hot, to be hot; Greek zestos (G2200), boiling hot.

expand to see more

Hebrew charah (H2734) — to burn, to be kindled, of wrath; Exodus 32:10–11, 32:19, 22:24.

Hebrew chamam (H2552) — to be hot, grow warm; Psalm 39:3, Exodus 16:21, Hosea 7:7.

Hebrew cham (H2525) — hot, warm; Joshua 9:12, Job 37:17.

Greek zestos (G2200) — boiling hot; Revelation 3:15–16 only.

Usage

"“Neither cold nor hot” — Laodicea's useless water."

"“That my wrath may wax hot” — and the intercessor did not deny it was just."

"“My heart was hot within me” — a fire that found its outlet in prayer."
